On Santiago Island, the rocks tell the story of its geological past. In Sullivan Bay, hardened lava forms waves and rope-like patterns. Cracks and folds left as the flow cooled are visible underfoot. Take time to appreciate the many shapes across a single dark lava field.

Near Puerto Egas, the walking route follows a rocky shore. Seawater fills hollows in the stone, while Galápagos fur seals rest in shaded grottoes. Marine iguanas and coastal birds can also be seen nearby. Espumilla Beach offers a different scene: its sandy shore is a nesting site for sea turtles, shifting attention from the rock formations to the signs of life along the ocean.

Each landing reveals another side of Santiago Island. The cruise itinerary determines which parts of the island you will see, and the varied shoreline makes each stop rewarding. Santiago will appeal to travelers who enjoy walking and wildlife watching and are happy to linger over small details in the landscape.

The cathedral is an active Catholic church and an important monument in Santiago's history. A visit is usually combined with views of neighboring historic buildings, the Central Post Office, and City Hall.

The square is an ideal place to appreciate the architecture. Entry depends on the church's opening arrangements and religious services; viewing the exterior does not guarantee access to the interior.
